When someone or something is victorious, it means they have won — they came out on top after a competition, battle, struggle, or contest of any kind. A victorious person, team, or side is the one that defeated the other side and claimed the win.

Think of it this way: if two teams play a football match and one team wins, that winning team is the victorious team.
What Makes It Deeper Than Just "Winning"

The word "victorious" carries a slightly stronger and more powerful feeling than simply saying "the winning side." It suggests that there was a real challenge, a real opponent, or a real struggle involved — and despite that, someone came out on top. It carries a sense of triumph and achievement. You wouldn't usually call someone "victorious" for winning a coin toss, because that involves no effort. But you would absolutely call an army "victorious" after a hard-fought battle, or an athlete "victorious" after defeating a tough opponent.

So built into this word is the idea of effort meeting success.

This adjective can describe a very wide range of subjects.

A person can be victorious — a boxer who knocks out his opponent, a politician who wins an election, a student who wins a debate competition.

A team or group can be victorious — a sports team that wins a championship, an army that wins a war, a political party that wins an election.

A nation or country can be victorious — as in, the Allies were victorious in World War II.

It can also describe expressions, feelings, or moments — a victorious smile, a victorious roar from the crowd, a victorious moment. Here, it describes something that reflects or belongs to the winner — the smile on someone's face that shows they've won.
How It Is Used in Sentences

"The victorious team lifted the trophy above their heads." — Here, it directly describes the team that won.

"She felt victorious after finally solving the problem she had struggled with for weeks." — Here, it describes her internal feeling of having overcome a personal challenge.

"The victorious army marched through the city." — Here, it describes an army that has won a battle or war.

"He flashed a victorious grin at his rival." — Here, it describes a grin that communicates "I won."

"Against all odds, the smaller nation emerged victorious." — "Emerged victorious" is a very common phrase meaning someone ended up as the winner, often after difficulty.
Important Nuance: There Must Be Opposition

"Victorious" specifically requires that there was something or someone to beat. It is not used for general success or achievement on its own. You wouldn't say someone is "victorious" for baking a great cake, because there was no opponent or contest. But you would say they were victorious in a baking competition if they won it.

This is what separates "victorious" from a word like "successful." Success is broad — you can succeed at many things with no opponent involved. But to be victorious, there has to be a competition, a conflict, a challenge, or an adversary that you overcame.

Triumphant is the closest synonym. It also means having won or succeeded, but it leans slightly more into the emotional side — the joy, the celebration, the glory of the win. "Victorious" is more factual (you won), while "triumphant" feels more celebratory (you won and you're on top of the world).

Winning is a more casual and everyday way of saying the same thing. "The winning team" and "the victorious team" mean the same thing, but "victorious" sounds more formal and carries more weight.

Dominant means someone who controls or overpowers the competition consistently. A dominant team may win many games, but "victorious" refers specifically to winning a particular contest.

Successful is broader and does not require an opponent, as explained above.

The direct opposite of victorious is defeated — the side that lost. Other opposites include losing, beaten, vanquished (a more formal/literary word for thoroughly beaten), and overcome (when used to describe someone who was overpowered by another).

Someone can be narrowly victorious — meaning they barely won, by a very slim margin. Or they can be decisively victorious — meaning they won clearly and convincingly, with no doubt. The word itself doesn't tell you how they won, so you often see it paired with adverbs or phrases that add that detail.
The Full Picture in One Summary

Victorious is an adjective that describes a person, group, or force that has won a competition, battle, conflict, or struggle — especially one that involved a real challenge or opponent. It carries a tone of achievement and triumph. It is more formal and weightier than simply saying "winning." It always implies there was opposition to be overcome. It can describe the winner themselves, or expressions, moments, and feelings that belong to the winner.
